subject: Anthropology
title: Homo Floresiensis
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Homo Floresiensis.

hook.text: In 2003, scientists found a tiny human skeleton on an Indonesian island. Three feet tall. Nicknamed the Hobbit.

buildup.text: Homo floresiensis lived on Flores Island until about 50,000 years ago, with a brain the size of a grapefruit.

discovery.text: Despite their small brains, they made stone tools and hunted dwarf elephants. Size doesn't equal intelligence.

twist.text: Island dwarfism may explain their size. Limited resources on islands can shrink large species over generations.

climax.text: Floresiensis proves that human evolution wasn't one march toward bigger bodies and brains. It branched wildly.

quiz.question: What is notable about Homo floresiensis?
options: They were very small and lived on an island

details.summary: Homo floresiensis, nicknamed the hobbit, was a small-bodied hominin discovered on the Indonesian island of Flores. Standing only about one meter tall with a tiny brain, it survived until roughly 50,000 years ago — challenging assumptions about the relationship between brain size and tool use.
details.whyItMatters: Homo floresiensis shocked paleoanthropology by showing that a tiny-brained hominin made tools and hunted cooperatively until surprisingly recently. It demonstrates that human evolution produced far more diversity than previously imagined.
takeaways: Homo floresiensis stood about one meter tall with a very small brain
It made stone tools and hunted despite its diminutive size
It survived until roughly 50,000 years ago on Flores island

faq.question: Why was Homo floresiensis so small?
faq.answer: Island dwarfism is the leading explanation — isolated on an island with limited resources, body size decreased over generations. This phenomenon is well documented in other island mammals. Alternatively, it may have descended from a small-bodied ancestral hominin rather than shrinking on the island.

faq.question: How could it make tools with such a small brain?
faq.answer: Brain size alone does not determine cognitive ability — brain organization and neural density matter too. Homo floresiensis apparently had sufficient cognitive capacity for tool manufacture and cooperative hunting despite a brain roughly the size of a chimpanzee's.
